newsitem.title: USA: Bias in hiring keeps blacks out of sales jobs-studies.
newsitem.headline: Bias in hiring keeps blacks out of sales jobs-studies.

text.p: Employers are turning down many black applicants for jobs in sales and related occupations where they would have to deal with predominantly white customers, a study by two university economists shows.
"There's an enormous difference in hiring practices between companies where customers are white and where customers are black," said economist Harry Holzer of Michigan State University.

Holzer and economist Keith Ihlanfeldt of Georgia State University in Atlanta concluded that hiring bias exists after surveying 3,200 businesses in metropolitan Atlanta, Boston, Detroit and Los Angeles.

"It might have to do with the degree of personal contact between the customer and the employee," Holzer speculated, "because we didn't see hiring differences in service or blue-collar jobs in these same companies to the same extent."

In businesses where 75 percent or more of the customers are white, only 4 percent of sales jobs are filled by blacks, the survey found. But blacks held 23 percent of all sales jobs in firms where whites make up just 50 percent to 75 percent of all customers, and blacks held 59 percent of sales jobs where most customers are black.

"Employers will cater to the preference of their customers," Holzer said. "If some fraction of their customers are in some way uncomfortable among blacks, especially black men, that may be enough for employers to act on (because) they believe the customer will drift to establishments they feel most comfortable in."

Whether the reluctance of white employers to put blacks in sales jobs is due to their own prejudice or to what they perceive to be the prejudice of their customers, Holzer said, "either way, to me, that's discrimination."
But two economists at the University of Rochester in New York state said it is not bias but the need for efficient communication that influences employers' hiring decisions.
"(It's) the firm's natural desire for efficiency (that) drives the selection of employees to mirror customer characteristics," write Stacy Kole and Glenn MacDonald.

"Individuals with similar characteristics communicate at lower cost," they stated in the June issue of Research Highlights, published by the university's Simon Graduate School of Business Administration.
According to data from the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics in Washington, black workers comprise 10.7 percent of the labor force but only 7.9 percent of those employed in sales jobs.

Moreover, said Bureau of Labor Statistics economist Tom Hale, blacks tend to be "overrepresented in the lowest-paying sales jobs, as far as status goes." For example, only 16.6 percent of whites in sales work as cashiers, compared with 38 percent of blacks.
A typical white sales person earns $652 per week; a black sales person $417 per week, Bureau of Labor Statistics figures showed.

As jobs migrate to communities where the customer base is predominantly white, Michigan State's Holzer said, it becomes harder for blacks to apply for work in sales and to get hired. This may be a factor accounting for part of blacks' difficulties landing sales jobs.

In Atlanta, Holzer noted, the percentage of the region's jobs located in black communities declined during the 1980s from 27 percent to 19 percent. Over the same period, jobs available in Detroit's black communities dropped from 31 percent to 22 percent.

Since black-owned firms, largely concentrated in inner cities, typically pay 10 percent to 20 percent less than white-owned firms, Holzer said, their black employees earn less than whites who perform similar jobs.
Hispanics also suffer from bias in hiring in contact positions, Holzer said, but not to the extent of blacks.
(Sherwood Ross is a free-lance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
